section_summary: This section centers on Herbert O. Yardley’s published account of American codebreaking and a proposed second book containing Japanese diplomatic messages. State Department correspondence records concern about publicity, publishers’ requests for guidance after the 1933 government records law, and the Department’s eventual refusal to authorize unrestricted sales while declining action over copies already printed. The opening pages contain a French-language Martinique newspaper with a discussion of Yardley’s revelations amid unrelated local news, advertisements, and fiction.

subfiles.title: L’Aurore newspaper issue and advertisements
subfiles.about: A Martinique newspaper issue includes a column criticizing American codebreaking disclosures by Yardley.
subfiles.summary: The French-language issue contains political commentary, local reports, notices, advertisements, and serialized fiction. Jean Bernard’s Parisian column recounts Yardley’s claims about the American Black Chamber, including decoded diplomatic telegrams at the Washington conference and alleged commercial espionage.

subfiles.title: Suppression of Indiscreet Books Is Not Easy in America
subfiles.about: A column explains why the United States did not suppress Yardley’s book after it revealed decoded Japanese messages.
subfiles.summary: The clipping appears twice, with page 90 incomplete and page 91 carrying the full text. Gilbert argues that suppression or prosecution would confirm Yardley’s account, while denial would be unconvincing to Japan.

subfiles.title: Telegram asking about a Yardley lecture
subfiles.about: Crail asks whether a women’s club should engage Yardley to lecture.
subfiles.summary: Crail asks for a confidential view of any public-interest objection.

subfiles.title: Reply to Congressman Crail
subfiles.about: The Department responds to Crail’s inquiry about a Yardley lecture.
subfiles.summary: Further discussion or publicity would serve no useful purpose.

subfiles.title: Suggested reply to Congressman Crail
subfiles.about: Staff suggest language for the reply to Crail.
subfiles.summary: The draft advises against further discussion or publicity.

subfiles.title: Yardley lecture notice and handwritten forwarding note
subfiles.about: Buff forwards a notice of Yardley’s Harvard Club lecture.
subfiles.summary: Buff calls attention to Yardley’s public reception and story.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Yardley lecture information
subfiles.about: Carr acknowledges Buff’s information about Yardley’s lecture.
subfiles.summary: The Department thanks Buff for the January lecture notice.

subfiles.title: New Book Being Prepared by Major Yardley
subfiles.about: A warning that Yardley’s proposed book could inflame Japanese opinion.
subfiles.summary: The writer urges every possible effort to prevent publication of Japanese secret telegrams.

subfiles.title: Return of Yardley correspondence
subfiles.from: E. Goodwin for W. P. Armstrong Jr.
subfiles.to: Division of Communications and Records files
subfiles.about: The Special Assistant’s office returns attached Yardley correspondence.
subfiles.summary: Returns the correspondence to the files.

subfiles.title: Report of manuscript offered to Macmillan
subfiles.about: A U.S. attorney reports that Macmillan received Yardley’s Japanese Diplomatic Secrets manuscript.
subfiles.summary: The attorney offers prompt access to the manuscript for government review before the publisher returns it.

subfiles.title: The Yardley Publications
subfiles.about: The legal adviser recounts a publisher’s counsel seeking guidance on a pending bill and existing copies of Yardley’s book.
subfiles.summary: Mr. Rabb says Bobbs-Merrill has unsold copies and a planned low-priced printing, but declined Yardley’s new manuscript. The adviser says any request for government authorization should await enactment of the bill.

subfiles.title: Cosmopolitan inquiry about Japanese Diplomatic Secrets
subfiles.about: Cosmopolitan asks whether any portion of Yardley’s unpublished manuscript could be printed.
subfiles.summary: MacBride asks for the Department’s opinion and permission for possible magazine publication.

subfiles.title: Reply to Cosmopolitan
subfiles.about: The Department answers Cosmopolitan’s inquiry about publishing Yardley’s manuscript.
subfiles.summary: Phillips says the claim that government prohibited publication is misleading, but the Department sees no American policy interest served by publishing any portion.

subfiles.title: Justice Department transmittal concerning Real Detective
subfiles.about: Justice forwards a report of an article about Yardley due in Real Detective.
subfiles.summary: The letter transmits material on “Spilling International Secrets” for possible action.

subfiles.title: Bobbs-Merrill request concerning The American Black Chamber
subfiles.about: The division reviews Bobbs-Merrill’s request for unrestricted permission to continue book sales.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes wide prior distribution and doubts a suppression attempt would be useful. It questions whether the Department should issue express permission; page 107 contains a brief, largely illegible handwritten note.

subfiles.title: Review note on draft reply
subfiles.about: Hornbeck suggests deleting a sentence from the draft reply.
subfiles.summary: Requests one final revision to the letter.

subfiles.title: Department reply to Bobbs-Merrill
subfiles.about: The Department declines to endorse continued distribution of Yardley’s book.
subfiles.summary: Phillips says the new law’s application to earlier publication and the identity of the competent authority are unclear. The Department will not issue a statement implying approval and suggests consulting Justice.

subfiles.title: Cover letter to Senator Van Nuys’s secretary
subfiles.about: Hornbeck sends Stern the Department’s reply to Chambers.
subfiles.summary: Encloses the reply and returns Chambers’s letter to the senator.

subfiles.title: Alternative draft reply to Bobbs-Merrill
subfiles.about: A draft would state no objection to continued sales of unchanged copies.
subfiles.summary: The draft questions the law’s application but proposes saying the Department has no objection to sales of the previously published text, while advising consultation with Justice.

subfiles.title: Chambers letter to Senator Van Nuys
subfiles.about: Chambers seeks rapid permission to continue sales of The American Black Chamber.
subfiles.summary: He cites sales and distribution already made, pending copies, financial and sales disruption, and a pledge to keep any permission confidential.

subfiles.title: Bobbs-Merrill petition to the Secretary of State
subfiles.from: D. L. Chambers for Bobbs-Merrill Company
subfiles.about: The publisher requests unrestricted authorization to continue sales of Yardley’s book.
subfiles.summary: The petition cites prior sales, an existing reprint contract, Yardley’s assurances about retained messages, refusal of his new manuscript, and potential financial loss.

subfiles.title: Yardley letter to Bobbs-Merrill
subfiles.about: Yardley explains how he obtained message copies used in his manuscript.
subfiles.summary: He claims telegraph company consent and knowledge by his government superiors.

subfiles.title: Bobbs-Merrill and Blue Ribbon Books reprint agreement
subfiles.about: The firms agree on a popular-priced reprint of The American Black Chamber.
subfiles.summary: The contract grants reprint sales rights, sets a minimum edition and royalties, and governs printing plates, accountings, pricing, replacements, and copyright notices.

subfiles.title: Legal Adviser’s view of Bobbs-Merrill request
subfiles.about: The legal adviser proposes more accommodating wording for the publisher’s reply.
subfiles.summary: He says the law aimed chiefly at Yardley’s proposed new code-message book, rather than sales already underway. He suggests stating no objection to continued sales of the unchanged earlier book, subject to consulting Justice.

subfiles.title: Routing note for Mr. Payer
subfiles.about: Phillips routes the official file for Payer to read.
subfiles.summary: Asks Payer to return it through Miss Newcombe.

subfiles.title: Attorney General’s referral of publisher petition
subfiles.about: Justice refers Bobbs-Merrill’s petition and gives its reading of the 1933 law.
subfiles.summary: The Attorney General argues that post-enactment furnishing of covered diplomatic material could fall within the law, including publisher assistance. He identifies the State Department as the competent authority to authorize or object.

subfiles.title: Bobbs-Merrill petition to the Attorney General
subfiles.from: D. L. Chambers for Bobbs-Merrill Company
subfiles.about: The publisher asks Justice to permit unrestricted continued sales.
subfiles.summary: The petition repeats the sales history, reprint obligations, Yardley’s assurances, rejection of the new manuscript, and anticipated loss if sales stop.

subfiles.title: Yardley letter to Bobbs-Merrill, second copy
subfiles.about: A second copy of Yardley’s explanation of the message copies used in his book.
subfiles.summary: Yardley claims consent from telegraph company presidents and knowledge by superiors.

subfiles.title: Reprint agreement, second copy
subfiles.about: A second copy of the reprint contract accompanies the petition to Justice.
subfiles.summary: It sets exclusive low-priced reprint rights, a minimum edition, royalties, and production terms.

subfiles.title: Cover letter to the Attorney General
subfiles.about: Phillips forwards the Department’s response to Bobbs-Merrill.
subfiles.summary: Encloses a copy of the letter to Chambers.

subfiles.title: Final State Department response to Bobbs-Merrill
subfiles.about: The Department refuses unrestricted permission for further publication and distribution of Yardley’s book.
subfiles.summary: Phillips says authorization would imply approval of a book the Department had not endorsed. The Department will take no action concerning copies actually printed before the June 14 petition, provided the publisher does not use the government correspondence for advertising, higher prices, or other purposes.
